findings.Quote: because because the alternative was to stop
findings.Note: duplicated word appears to be a typo, but even corrected the clause is a flat abstraction stating the discipline rather than dramatizing it
findings.Fix: cut to 'because stopping wasn't an order he'd been given.'

findings.Quote: The room went very still.
findings.Note: Stock tension-beat phrasing used elsewhere in the manuscript's tradition; adds nothing concrete here.
findings.Fix: Cut the sentence or replace with a specific physical detail (e.g., who looked where).

findings.Quote: Declan wasn't a liar. Declan was something more expensive than a liar.
findings.Note: Aphoristic flourish that sounds clever but doesn't clarify anything concrete about Declan; purple pseudo-profundity standing in for characterization.
findings.Fix: Cut the second sentence, or replace with a concrete behavioral detail that shows the distinction.

findings.Quote: He sat up before he decided to.
findings.Note: body-acts-before-mind beat is a stock device, reinforced by the immediately following explicit restatement
findings.Fix: keep one instance of the idea, cut the redundant follow-up sentence

findings.Quote: lived in him now the way an old break lives in a bone — set, healed, load-bearing, and plain to anyone who knew where to look
findings.Note: Extended bone-break metaphor for old habits/training is a well-worn device, and stacking it onto the uniform metaphor already made a sentence earlier is redundant.
findings.Fix: Cut the simile and let the preceding 'couldn't take eleven years of standing at attention out of his spine' carry the point alone.

findings.Quote: Not money. Money would have been easy; money you spend down and refill. This was the other kind of price.
findings.Note: Explains the metaphor it's about to make (favors vs money) in flat aphoristic terms before earning it — tells the reader the lesson instead of trusting the following details to carry it.
findings.Fix: Cut the setup sentences and let 'the specific kind of favor that lives in one person' open the paragraph directly.

findings.Quote: the count, the times, the entry on the woman in the second-floor window
findings.Note: The stated purpose is to build the human reality of the forty-three through sustained detail of the lit window, but the woman and window are only referenced abstractly here, not rendered in sensory detail; the beat asserts her significance rather than making her presence undeniable.
findings.Fix: Include at least one concrete sensory detail of the window/woman (light, posture, action) rather than a bare label.

findings.Quote: the Manowar humming warm against his sternum like a leash that held on tight
findings.Note: mixed/strained simile — a leash doesn't hum or sit warm against a sternum, and 'held on tight' is redundant with leash's inherent meaning; the image doesn't hold up to literal scrutiny
findings.Fix: cut to something concrete: 'the Manowar's compliance lock, warm against his sternum, a leash he'd stopped noticing he wore'

findings.Quote: He didn't ask whether it could be done.
findings.Note: The purpose is to show Bear's counter-move being revealed as clever/decisive, but this line just asserts confidence without demonstrating the mechanism or stakes of the counter-move beyond the manifest/exhibit pairing already stated.
findings.Fix: Trim or fold into the surrounding action rather than flagging it as a standalone assertion.

findings.Quote: a man signing every line of a long document instead of initialing the bottom
findings.Fix: cut or replace with a sharper, less explanatory image

findings.Quote: let himself feel the shape of her — the fact of her, a person with opinions about where money should go — for the length of the pause
findings.Fix: tighten to avoid abstraction ('the shape of her,' 'the fact of her') diluting the concrete farewell-ritual purpose

findings.Quote: a body that never moved read as a thing instead of a man
findings.Fix: tighten to something less axiomatic, e.g. 'a body that never moved looked like it was waiting for something'

findings.Quote: Somewhere far off, the Spine droned — the kind of sound you stopped hearing, like your own blood.
findings.Note: the 'sound like your own blood/heartbeat' comparison is a familiar sensory-numbness trope
findings.Fix: cut the simile or replace with a more specific, non-bodily comparison

findings.Quote: That mark was its own kind of weather
findings.Note: vague metaphor that doesn't hold up to literal scrutiny — weather isn't a good vehicle for experience-level in a unit
findings.Fix: cut or replace with a more concrete comparison

findings.Quote: the way you keep a hand near something hot
findings.Note: stock cautionary-attention image
findings.Fix: replace with a more specific tactical detail

findings.Quote: a door he'd left on the latch, finally pushed
findings.Note: tidy metaphor stating the emotional turn rather than dramatizing it
findings.Fix: cut or ground it in a concrete sensory beat

findings.Quote: useless as weather when it came to minding who was in the road
findings.Note: second weather-as-metaphor construction in close proximity across beats, and reads as a filler aphorism about the Behemoths
findings.Fix: simplify to a literal description of the cargo unit's indifference

findings.Quote: a large man taking up the room a large man takes up
findings.Note: circular, low-content phrasing that reads as filler rather than characterization
findings.Fix: cut the tautology; describe the specific way he occupies space

findings.Quote: You don't decide to trust the floor you're standing on.
findings.Note: aphoristic filler that states the theme rather than dramatizing it
findings.Fix: cut or replace with a concrete detail showing the trust in action

findings.Quote: he said it to himself the way other men said grace — plainly, because it was true.
findings.Note: the tacked-on 'because it was true' is an assertion of truth rather than earned demonstration, slightly undercutting the otherwise strong distinction just drawn
findings.Fix: end the sentence at 'plainly' and let the grace comparison carry it

findings.Quote: It was the feeling of a man who has carried something in one direction for four years and finds it has been moving in another direction the whole time, on its own, without him.
findings.Note: tells the emotional payoff in abstract, essay-like terms instead of trusting the concrete scene (the line item, the cold cup) already doing the work
findings.Fix: cut the sentence and let the preceding image (cold cup, three readings of the line) carry the beat

findings.Quote: He knew the number was imprecise... fear flattens the difference between one and several
findings.Note: the beat's purpose is to show the count as involuntary and pre-conscious, but this passage has him analytically reasoning about statistical error, which reads as deliberate cognition rather than something his training did to him against his will
findings.Fix: trim the explanatory clause on fear/acoustics and let the imprecision surface only through sensory confusion, not analysis

findings.Quote: that was the part he would carry every twenty-first after — that he had don
findings.Note: text is cut off mid-word, leaving the sentence incomplete
findings.Fix: complete the sentence

findings.Quote: the way a man looks at weather he means to walk through
findings.Note: stock 'weathering it' metaphor for stoic resolve
findings.Fix: replace with a more specific, non-idiomatic image tied to Bear's actual sensory world

findings.Quote: worn smooth as a coin
findings.Note: familiar comparison used as filler texture rather than earning its place
findings.Fix: cut or replace with a detail specific to the leverage itself

findings.Quote: so you stop loving them before they kill you
findings.Note: aphoristic flourish attributed to Brandt that reads as a scripted 'wise mentor' line rather than something a real officer would say
findings.Fix: cut the clause or make it plainer, e.g. 'so you don't waste time defending the bad ones'

findings.Quote: He didn't know her name. He had chosen not to know it, which was a different thing from not knowing it, and the difference had kept him decent for eight years.
findings.Note: the distinction is asserted as profound but is a semantic trick restating itself rather than showing the moral weight
findings.Fix: cut the middle clause and let 'He had chosen not to know it' carry the meaning alone

findings.Quote: He hadn't thought about it in exactly those terms before. He was thinking about it now.
findings.Note: beat purpose calls for the girl's existence to complicate the escape plan, but this closing pair of flat sentences tells us he's reflecting rather than dramatizing the complication's actual pull on his decision
findings.Fix: replace with a concrete statement of what the testimony now costs him in the escape calculus

findings.Quote: He felt it land below his sternum, a small click.
findings.Note: The below-the-sternum physical tell for realization is a familiar bodily-cue shorthand bordering on stock phrasing.
findings.Fix: Replace with a more specific, non-generic reaction unique to Bear's professional read of the call.

findings.Quote: He'd used a few himself.
findings.Note: Slightly glib aside that undercuts the tension with a wink of narrator-cool rather than deepening characterization.
findings.Fix: Cut or fold into the surrounding analysis without the quip beat.

findings.Quote: She was reading him the way the gate guard had, but the other way around. Not deciding to be blind. Deciding to see.
findings.Note: Neat rhetorical parallel that feels constructed for symmetry rather than earned observation — slightly too pleased with its own structure.
findings.Fix: Cut the explicit callback and let the guard/fiduciary parallel remain implicit.

findings.Quote: He held it, with his whole chest, no flinching, the size of him not quite fitting the client chair.
findings.Note: Vague physical description ('with his whole chest') gestures at emotional weight without concretely showing it — borders on telling.
findings.Fix: Specify a concrete physical detail (e.g., how his hands rested, how still he kept them) instead of the abstract 'whole chest.'

findings.Quote: the world's steady failure to picture him in advance
findings.Note: Slightly overwritten aphoristic phrasing for a simple observation (furniture never fits him), tipping into cleverness rather than plain procedural grounding the beat calls for.
findings.Fix: Simplify to something like 'the world's habit of not planning for a man his size.'

findings.Quote: He did exactly that much and no more — the way you move furniture out of a doorway, without looking at it and without breaking sentence.
findings.Note: The furniture-moving simile undercuts the physical danger/violence of the moment with a domestic, faintly comic image that reads as authorial cleverness rather than in-scene tension.
findings.Fix: Cut the simile or replace with something that preserves menace, e.g., 'He cleared them the way he cleared a doorway — without looking, without breaking sentence.'

findings.Quote: A trained compliance grip needs the other man to move against it. Bear did not.
findings.Note: Reads as inserted technical exposition/aphorism about grappling mechanics rather than embedded action; slows the climax to explain technique.
findings.Fix: Show the effect without the explanatory rule: 'The lead's grip needed him to pull back. He didn't.'

findings.Quote: the way he shook any hand — present, complete, no agenda
findings.Note: Repeats almost verbatim a few lines later in the excerpt ('present and complete, the way he shook any hand' appears again in beat 2), reading as a canned tic rather than a deliberate motif on first exposure.
findings.Fix: Vary the phrasing or trim the repetition to one instance across the two beats.

findings.Quote: the open hand of a man who had just finished being a soldier, held out across the distance between what they had been and what the morning had made of them
findings.Note: Overwritten abstraction stacked onto a simple gesture; tells rather than shows the weight of the moment.
findings.Fix: Cut to the concrete image: 'Brandt looked at the hand for one full second before he took it.'

findings.Quote: Relief was for men who had been afraid, and he had spent his fear years ago, on a morning at Cortland, in a currency that did not come back.
findings.Note: Aphoristic construction ('relief was for men who...') with a purple 'currency' metaphor that doesn't hold up literally — fear as spent currency is vague rather than illuminating.
findings.Fix: Cut the metaphor and state plainly: 'This wasn't relief — he'd used up his fear years ago, at Cortland.'

findings.Quote: He looked for the institution in himself and found it gone.
findings.Note: Tells the reader the internal state abstractly rather than dramatizing it; borders on pseudo-profound shorthand.
findings.Fix: Ground it in a concrete detail — e.g., what specifically he checked for and didn't find (a habit, a reflex) rather than the abstract 'the institution in himself.'

findings.Quote: the cool outside air came up against his beard and the open part of his chest like the first true thing in hours
findings.Note: Purple simile leaning on vague 'truth' abstraction rather than concrete sensation; doesn't survive literal scrutiny (air isn't 'true').
findings.Fix: Replace with a direct sensory beat: 'the cool air hit his beard and the open part of his chest.'

findings.Quote: a man learns young not to reach for his own heart in front of strangers; they read it wrong
findings.Note: Aphoristic generalization stated as universal truth — filler-wisdom tone that slows the immediate bodily beat.
findings.Fix: Cut the generalization; keep the action: 'He kept his hand at his side. There were people on the steps below him.'

findings.Quote: a sound like something breathing through cloth
findings.Note: purple/vague simile for a fan noise that doesn't sharpen the image much, mild reach for atmosphere
findings.Fix: cut or make more literal: 'a low mechanical rasp'

findings.Quote: It didn't have to be right. It only had to hold long enough to matter.
findings.Note: aphoristic construction ('didn't have to be X, only had to Y') is a familiar rhetorical pattern bordering on stock wisdom-quip
findings.Fix: tighten into plainer observation without the symmetrical maxim structure

findings.Quote: A loading dock has two lives, and the early one is honest.
findings.Fix: cut the aphorism or ground it in a concrete observation instead of a stated maxim

findings.Quote: Deferred maintenance was its own kind of map.
findings.Fix: cut; the metaphor restates the previous paragraph's point without adding anything

findings.Quote: the way you give a dog the slow hand before the fast one
findings.Fix: replace with an image specific to Bear's own trade rather than a generic dog-training simile

findings.Quote: patience, which is a different muscle, and Bear had the larger one
findings.Fix: cut or replace; reads as a stock tough-guy aphorism rather than earned insight

findings.Quote: He felt it land before any alert could — the small clean click of a thing he'd planned arriving exactly where he'd set it down.
findings.Fix: trim the redundant restatement ('felt it land,' 'small clean click,' 'arriving exactly where he'd set it down') to one concrete image

findings.Quote: the sentence already smooth from the night he'd spent sanding it
findings.Note: Cute but unverifiable authorial assertion presented as fact — tells us Declan rehearsed rather than showing it.
findings.Fix: Let the smoothness show through delivery/rhythm rather than asserting the rehearsal history.

findings.Quote: the way you know weather
findings.Note: Familiar comparison, softens the sharper characterization work happening around it.
findings.Fix: Replace with a more specific, non-idiomatic comparison tied to Bear's own history with Declan.

findings.Quote: He'd been a discovery. A late one.
findings.Note: fragment pileup that states the beat's thesis flatly rather than dramatizing it — borders on telling-not-showing the recontextualization the beat purpose demands
findings.Fix: integrate into the surrounding sentence rather than isolating as a stark aphorism-like fragment

findings.Quote: not pain, just the structure reporting it was still there and could still take the load
findings.Note: abstract engineering metaphor for emotion tells rather than shows
findings.Fix: replace with a concrete physical detail instead of the load-bearing abstraction

findings.Quote: The recognition landed before he'd finished taking it in — the old pull toward the man, quick and unwelcome.
findings.Note: Tells the reader Bear feels a pull rather than showing it through action or detail; vague abstraction dropped into an otherwise concrete physical description.
findings.Fix: Cut or replace with a physical tell (a held breath, a stalled step) that dramatizes the pull.

findings.Quote: It was a great deal of effort to put between yourself and a handshake.
findings.Fix: cut or sharpen; lands as a wry aphorism rather than earned character insight

findings.Quote: Exactly as fast as years of practice make a man. Which meant exactly as fast as Bear had planned for, because the speed practice gives you is the speed it gives everyone, and Bear had counted on the average.
findings.Fix: cut the repetitive 'exactly as fast' construction and the generalized-truth phrasing; state the tactical fact once

findings.Quote: The cost wasn't abstract. It had names too.
findings.Note: Tacked-on aphoristic closer restating the point already made concretely by 'Brandt was spending people Bear had once stood beside.'
findings.Fix: Cut the final two sentences; end on 'Brandt was spending people Bear had once stood beside.'

findings.Quote: like a screen turned down one step too f
findings.Note: Truncated simile (cut off mid-word) — as delivered it's an incomplete, unreadable image.
findings.Fix: Complete the sentence or cut the fragment.

findings.Quote: A relay that announced its own failure would frighten its user, and a frightened user made decisions, and decisions were variables.
findings.Note: Aphoristic, slightly pseudo-profound triplet construction that explains the device's logic in a stock 'wisdom' cadence rather than showing it.
findings.Fix: Compress to a single plain technical sentence: 'The NS-7 was built not to announce failure — a frightened user makes decisions, and decisions are variables.'

findings.Quote: a decision already furnished
findings.Note: clever-sounding phrase that doesn't quite parse literally — a room can be furnished, a decision cannot be 'furnished' in any concrete sense; reads as reaching for profundity
findings.Fix: replace with something grounded: 'The door didn't open on a room so much as a choice already made for him'

findings.Quote: A field log doesn't editorialize. It gives the time, the position, the count, the thing seen — and it lets a reader who wasn't there stand where the writer stood and see what he saw.
findings.Note: Explains the metaphor's function rather than trusting the reader to infer it from the ensuing testimony; slightly didactic for a beat meant to demonstrate discipline through action.
findings.Fix: Cut the explanatory second sentence and let the testimony itself prove the discipline.

findings.Quote: he knew the warmth he carried into a room and he knew that warmth could carry a panel a long way if he let it
findings.Note: 'Warmth could carry a panel' is a soft, vague abstraction standing in for a more concrete characterization of his charisma.
findings.Fix: Specify what the warmth does — e.g., 'he knew panels liked him, that a joke here or a modest pause there could soften a verdict' — or cut.

findings.Quote: You learn to read an order the way you learn to read weather.
findings.Note: Stock analogy/aphorism construction ('you learn to read X the way you learn to read weather') that feels like inserted wisdom rather than character-specific observation.
findings.Fix: Replace with a more concrete, non-generic comparison drawn from his own experience, e.g., 'I read the order the way I read a perimeter — for what was missing.'

findings.Quote: which told him she understood that something was being built
findings.Note: Telling the reader the significance of the investigator's gesture instead of letting the gesture (stylus poised, not writing) carry it.
findings.Fix: Cut the explanatory clause and let the action stand alone.

findings.Quote: twelve hundred pounds of powered steel placed like a man stepping around a sleeping dog
findings.Note: simile strains scale and register — a 1200lb war frame being compared to tiptoeing around a dog undercuts the tension of the moment
findings.Fix: replace with a more proportionate image of controlled mass, e.g. 'placed like something that had learned to apologize for its own weight'

findings.Quote: He looked at it the way you look at a door you've just locked — checking with your eyes because your hand already knows it's locked, and the hand isn't the part of you that needs convincing
findings.Note: overextended simile that explains itself twice, tipping into telling rather than trusting the image
findings.Fix: cut the second clause and let 'checking with your eyes' stand alone

findings.Quote: He read them the way he'd once read a perimeter — not looking for a line that flattered him, looking for a weak one.
findings.Note: Slightly overwrought comparison that tells us how to feel about his diligence rather than showing it through action.
findings.Fix: Cut the simile; let the reading stand on its own: 'He wasn't looking for a line that flattered him. He was looking for a weak one.'

findings.Quote: Forty-three people, fit into a sentence with room to spare, leaving no sign they'd ever been there.
findings.Note: Slightly reaches for poetic effect ('room to spare') in a beat that otherwise earns its restraint through plain fact.
findings.Fix: Trim to 'Forty-three people, fit into a sentence, leaving no sign they'd ever been there.'

findings.Quote: read off his specs the way a man reads a menu aloud — no boast in it, just laying out what was on the table
findings.Note: the menu simile and 'laying out what was on the table' double up on the same idea (listing items plainly), slightly redundant phrasing
findings.Fix: pick one: either the menu image or 'laying out what was on the table,' not both

findings.Quote: A panel has a sound to it, the way a building does.
findings.Note: A purple simile that doesn't clarify or add sensory precision — buildings don't have a distinctive 'sound' in any way that illuminates what a panel sounds like.
findings.Fix: Cut the simile and go straight to the concrete details: 'Chairs. The scratch of a stylus...'

findings.Quote: the frost not quite burned off it, the kind of ground that holds the cold a little longer than the air does
findings.Note: Overwrought nature-writing flourish that slows the momentum right before the emotional crux, reads as reaching for atmosphere rather than plain log-style report consistent with the character's established voice.
findings.Fix: Trim to something plainer: 'Flat, frost still on it.'

findings.Quote: I have learned that when a man is about to say a thing he has decided to say, the room around him goes very ordinary, and you remember the ordinary parts.
findings.Note: Reads as an inserted aphorism about memory/rooms rather than something a witness would naturally say; slightly too polished/generalized for testimony voice.
findings.Fix: Cut to something plainer: 'I remember the ordinary parts. I don't know why, but I do.'

findings.Quote: A man can say forty-three dead and mean it, and everyone in the tent would have understood him.
findings.Note: Slides into a generalized truism about language rather than staying anchored in the specific testimony, softening the sharp forensic focus of the beat.
findings.Fix: Tighten to the specific: 'He could have said forty-three dead. Nobody would have misunderstood him.'

findings.Quote: He read that sentence three times, the way he'd once read a yellow flag on a briefing slide — a small square of color at the corner of something bigger, put there to be moved past.
findings.Note: Simile is doing a lot of abstract work and doesn't clarify the actual sensory or emotional beat; reads as reaching for gravitas rather than showing his reaction.
findings.Fix: Cut the simile or ground it in a concrete memory beat instead of an abstracted metaphor.

findings.Quote: the kind of economy he'd have respected in a soldier
findings.Note: Vague characterizing aside that tells rather than shows, and slightly clichéd military-respect framing.
findings.Fix: Cut, or replace with a specific detail about what the brevity meant to him.

findings.Quote: at the speed of nothing happening, until everything happened at once
findings.Note: Stock construction for describing time passing unevenly.
findings.Fix: Replace with a more specific, non-formulaic description of the waiting.

findings.Quote: she'd started to feel like the surveillance was the thing being tested, not the target
findings.Note: Slightly pseudo-profound aphorism dropped into dialogue-report; reads as a thematic statement more than something a tired agent would actually say.
findings.Fix: Make it more concrete/specific to the situation rather than a general observation.

findings.Quote: cleaned the way a man who'd once lived rough cleans — swept, aired, the cot stripped down to the frame
findings.Note: The 'cleaned the way X cleans' construction is a familiar rhetorical device bordering on cliché, though the specifics redeem it somewhat.
findings.Fix: Tighten to just the concrete details without the framing generalization.

findings.Quote: Not dropped. Placed — the way you set down a thing you've decided is finished with you, and want found in a certain order.
findings.Note: Slightly overwrought explanation of a gesture that the following sentences already dramatize concretely (face-down, blank back first); the abstraction undercuts the sharper image right after it.
findings.Fix: Cut the generalized 'the way you set down...' clause and let the concrete sequence carry the meaning.

findings.Quote: put his hand flat on his chest one more time — no warmth, no cycle, just the frame, steady under his palm
findings.Note: Gesture reads as a stock introspective/emotional beat (hand-to-chest) even though it's recontextualized with cyberpunk body detail; the 'steady under his palm' lands close to heartbeat-symbolism cliché territory.
findings.Fix: Vary the gesture or cut the repetition of this motif if it's been used earlier in the manuscript to signify resolve.

findings.Quote: It was never mine to carry alone
findings.Note: Reads as a tidy aphoristic rejoinder — thematically neat but slightly too polished/quotable for the naturalistic dialogue around it.
findings.Fix: Make the line more specific to the sixteen names or dock relationships rather than a general statement.
